title: Fill a bucket to the brim from a garden hose's trigger nozzle, then stop the water
instruction: Pick up the hose nozzle, fill the blue bucket to the brim with it, then stop the water. Don't let it overflow or spill.
context: Filling a bucket from a hose is an everyday yard chore (washing a car, mixing, watering, animal water). It takes a tool picked up off the ground with a hose dragging on it, aimed with one hand and run with the other through a sprung trigger, and a stop timed by watching the water rise: too early leaves it short, too late runs it over.
setup: Two YAM arms at the station table, each arm (links and gripper housing, not the fingers or the wrist cameras' lenses) and its base in a clear polyethylene splash sleeve. On the table is a black HDPE drip tray (816 x 1,224 mm outside, 2 mm floor, 35 mm walls; x 0.092-0.908 m, y -0.612-0.612 m; arm bases at x 0, y +-0.305), and in it a patio of 200 x 200 x 12 mm grey concrete pavers in running bond (ground surface 14 mm above the table, x 0.10-0.90 m, y -0.60-0.60 m). A blue polypropylene pail (0.38 kg empty; inside 180 mm across at the floor and 220 mm at the brim, 200 mm deep, brimful 6.30 L; rolled rim, one stiffening rib, steel wire bail lying down on its -x side) stands empty and free on the pavers, centred at (0.46, -0.04). A brick pillar 115 x 115 x 244 mm with a brass hose tap (handwheel red, nose pointing down 179 mm above the ground) stands at (0.66, 0.50); the tap is open throughout. Screwed onto the tap's nose is a digital garden-hose water meter (grey housing 48 mm across and 58 mm tall, LCD facing the robot, blue 3/4 inch swivel inlet holding a pressure-compensating 12 L/min flow-regulator washer, brass male outlet 95 mm above the ground). A 1.24 m green 5/8 inch garden hose (22 mm outside, 0.35 kg/m full of water) runs from the meter's outlet in a loop over the pavers (left of the pail) to the nozzle. The nozzle is a pistol-grip spray nozzle (0.24 kg; satin zinc barrel, green rubber grip on the barrel 44 mm long with flats 28 mm apart, green rubber handle 100 mm long hanging behind the barrel, brass hose swivel at the handle's foot, 52 mm pattern dial set to flood, outlet 10 mm) with a 25 g chrome trigger hinged under the barrel in front of the handle. The trigger's return spring holds it against its rest with 0.26 N m and takes 0.75 N m at its 22 deg stop; water starts at 6 deg of squeeze and is fully on (12 L/min) from 20 deg. The nozzle lies on its left side on the pavers, its barrel's grip centred at (0.300, 0.150), the barrel pointing back and to the left (turned 120 deg from straight ahead), the handle toward the robot's right. Code (parts.py) gives every dimension and pose.
scoring: The water is accounted for, in simulation and in a real trial alike: metered = litres that left the hose (the water meter's total); in the pail = litres the pail holds; spilled = metered - in the pail (whatever missed the pail, ran over its brim or splashed out). Full: at least 5.73 L in the pail (its surface within 15 mm of the brim). Score 0 if the pail tips more than 15 deg at any moment, or if more than 1.0 L is spilled. Otherwise 1.0 if the pail is full, the water has been off (trigger released past 6 deg, the meter not counting) for at least 1 s, and at most 0.25 L has been spilled; else 0.75 with at least 85% of the brimful volume in the pail (5.36 L), 0.5 with at least 50% (3.15 L), 0.25 with at least 25% (1.58 L), and 0 below that. The simulation reads these from its state: the meter's total is the nozzle's flow summed every control step, the pail's water is its contents. A real trial reads them with: the digital water meter between the tap and the hose (totalising, reads to 0.01 L, counts from 1 L/min or less), calibrated before each session against the scale; a bench scale (10 kg capacity, 1 g resolution) for the pail before and after (1 kg = 1 L; full = at least 5.73 kg of water); and the recorded video for the pail's tilt and the trigger's release. The tap stays open and the nozzle closed at the start and the end, so the hose holds the same water both times and the meter's count all left through the nozzle. Measurement error after calibration is about 0.06 L, a quarter of the 0.25 L limit.
run_limit: 1,600 control steps at 20 Hz (80 s). The scripted demo reaches full score at 47.4 s.
reset_notes: Empty and dry the pail; weigh it empty (0.38 kg) and note the meter's reading before each trial. Lay the hose back in its loop and the nozzle on its side at the start pose (see setup.png); the trigger is sprung and returns by itself. Wipe the pavers and grippers dry (spilled water stays in the drip tray and is not collected for scoring). Use object_jitter=0 for the fixed layout. Real trials, once a session: bleed the hose's air into a spare bucket; check the flow (a 30 s full squeeze into the pail gives 6.0 +- 0.3 L by the scale); calibrate the meter (three full-flow fills of about 6 L into the pail, each weighed; correction factor = weighed / metered; the three fills must agree within 0.05 L). Keep the arm and base sleeves on, the drip tray under the patio, and the power supplies and controllers off the table and out of the tray.
fidelity: Hose: 31 rigid links with sprung, damped joints; nozzle, sprung trigger and pail are rigid bodies held by contact. Water is not a fluid simulation: flow follows the trigger's angle (12 L/min at full squeeze), the stream is traced ballistically and counted into or out of the pail; water above the brim runs over. The meter totals the flow. Not modelled: splashing (a real trial counts it as spilled), sloshing, water in the hose. Tray and meter are fixed; sleeves are visual only.
